slides.heading: What is a satellite?
slides.text: A satellite is anything that travels around a planet in a loop called an orbit. The Moon is Earth's natural satellite!

slides.heading: Why doesn't it fall down?
slides.text: It does fall! But it also moves sideways so fast, about 28,000 km/h (17,500 mph), that it keeps missing the ground. Isaac Newton imagined this with a cannon on a very tall mountain.

slides.heading: Satellites help us every day
slides.text: Today, satellites help us forecast the weather, watch TV, find our way with maps, make phone calls, and look after Earth's forests and oceans.

slides.heading: Back to 1958
slides.text: Let's travel back to 1958, three years before Freedom 7. The Soviet Union had already launched Sputnik, and the United States wanted to launch a satellite too.

slides.heading: Meet Explorer 1
slides.text: Explorer 1 was built at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in California. JPL became part of NASA later that same year.

image.alt: Workers attaching Explorer 1 to the top of its rocket

slides.credit: Photo: NASA · Explorer 1 being attached to its rocket

slides.heading: Launch!
slides.text: On January 31, 1958, a Juno I rocket launched Explorer 1 from Cape Canaveral, Florida. Here is a NASA film about Explorer 1 and everything that came after it.

video.credit: Video: NASA Goddard · Explorer 1: Celebrating 60 Years

slides.heading: A science mission
slides.text: Explorer 1 carried an experiment by Dr. James Van Allen to count tiny, fast particles in space. It was about 2 m (80 in) long and weighed about 14 kg (30.8 lb).

slides.heading: Your mission
slides.text: Let's put Explorer 1 together, guide it into orbit, and keep it steady up there!

Drag each part from the parts box onto the matching shape. I'll tell you what each part does!
assembly.doneLine: Explorer 1 is complete! A small satellite with a big job: measuring space around Earth.

parts.name: Rocket Motor
parts.info: The last rocket stage. It gave the final push into orbit and stayed attached to Explorer 1.

parts.name: Whip Antennas
parts.info: Four long, bendy antennas helped send radio signals. Their wobbling later made Explorer 1 tumble!

parts.name: Batteries
parts.info: Batteries powered the science instruments and radios. They lasted until May 1958.

parts.name: Radio Transmitters
parts.info: Two small radios sent the science readings down to Earth as radio signals.

parts.name: Cosmic Ray Detector
parts.info: A Geiger counter that counted tiny, fast particles in space. It found the Van Allen radiation belts!

parts.name: Micrometeorite Detector
parts.info: Thin wires and a tiny microphone that noticed hits from specks of space dust.

parts.name: Nose Cone
parts.info: Protects the instruments during launch. Sensors inside measured temperature, and the stripes helped keep it not too hot and not too cold.

explorerReveal.line: Here is Explorer 1! It spun like a spinning top to stay steady. Drag to spin it around, then let's launch it!

intro: Rockets don't fly straight up to reach orbit. They slowly tip over and fly sideways, faster and faster.
Steer the rocket along the glowing path. Use the arrow keys, or touch the screen where you want it to go. Watch the TVs light up as you climb!
orbit.steerBack: Steer back to the glowing path!
orbit.resultText: You stayed on the path {pct}% of the time.
orbit.resultMore: Satellites like Explorer 1 started a revolution. The TVs show some of what came next!

tvs.name: Explorer 1
tvs.fact: America's first satellite sends radio beeps and science data.

tvs.name: TIROS-1
tvs.fact: The first successful weather satellite sends TV pictures of clouds.

tvs.name: Telstar 1
tvs.fact: The first live TV pictures sent across the Atlantic Ocean by satellite.

tvs.name: Syncom 3
tvs.fact: A satellite high above one spot helps send the Tokyo Olympics to TVs in America.

tvs.name: Landsat 1
tvs.fact: The first satellite made to photograph Earth's land. It is still helping scientists today through newer Landsats.

tvs.name: GPS
tvs.fact: The first GPS satellite launches. Today GPS helps maps find where you are.

intro: Explorer 1 had no thrusters. It spun like a pencil to stay steady, but its bendy antennas slowly wasted that spin, and it started to tumble end over end! Engineers learned from this when they designed later satellites.
Many modern satellites DO have tiny thrusters. Let's pretend Explorer 1 had some! Tap when the white marker is inside the green zone to push the satellite back onto its orbit.
balance.tooFar: Oh no, it drifted too far! Let's bring it back and try again.
balance.resultText: Great timing! Real satellites use small puffs like these to stay exactly where they belong. It's called station keeping.

slides.heading: A big discovery
slides.text: Explorer 1's Geiger counter found belts of fast particles trapped by Earth's magnetism. They are called the Van Allen radiation belts, after Dr. James Van Allen.

slides.heading: The first launch photo
slides.text: Here is the real Juno I rocket carrying Explorer 1 into the night sky on January 31, 1958.

slides.heading: Explorer 1 by the numbers
slides.text: It sent science data until its batteries ran out in May 1958, but it kept circling Earth until March 31, 1970, more than 58,000 times!

slides.heading: A whole family of Explorers
slides.text: Explorer 1 was the first of many. NASA has launched many more Explorer missions since, and thousands of satellites now circle our planet.
